analysis.one_liner: Limits courts' power to keep health and safety hazards secret in lawsuit settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote; it sat in the Judiciary Committee from May 2014 until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often settle lawsuits over dangerous products, drugs, or practices on the condition that the evidence stays hidden — courts issue 'protective orders' and approve settlements with gag terms, so other customers never learn about the hazard. This bill would require a judge to make specific findings before sealing such information, and would block settlements from preventing people from reporting hazards to federal or state safety regulators. It preserves confidentiality for private personal information and for classified national security material.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers who would learn about hidden health and safety hazards through court records and settlement disclosures; also whistleblowers and journalists who could report on dangers documented in litigation without facing contempt or breach-of-settlement penalties.

how_it_helps.text: In any civil case where the pleadings raise public health or safety issues, a court could not issue a secrecy order, seal court records, or approve a settlement that hides information unless it first finds the public's interest in disclosure is outweighed by a specific and substantial confidentiality interest, and that the order is no broader than necessary.

Courts could not enforce settlement terms that stop a party from reporting relevant information to any federal or state agency that regulates the activity — so a hazard documented in a lawsuit could reach the FDA, NHTSA, CPSC, or state regulators even after a confidential settlement.

Courts could not enforce settlement terms barring a party from disclosing that a settlement occurred or discussing the case and the evidence in it, when the matters involve public health or safety — the amount paid could stay confidential.

It protects privacy: the bill creates a rebuttable presumption that protecting an individual's financial or health information outweighs disclosure, and it explicitly leaves classified national defense information and intelligence sources and methods out of scope.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, companies defending lawsuits over product safety, drug effects, and workplace hazards would face harder-to-hide evidence, more public settlements, and more reports to regulators; they would lose a tool they use to contain litigation risk and reputational damage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defendants in health and safety lawsuits

drawbacks.text: Courts would have to hold additional fact-finding proceedings before issuing protective orders, adding time and cost to litigation that is already slow and expensive, and some judges and defendants argue parties should be free to settle privately on whatever terms they agree to.

Businesses argue that protective orders also shield legitimate trade secrets and competitive information disclosed in discovery, and that a mandatory findings process could chill settlements of legitimate claims; the bill mitigates this with its personal-information presumption and national-security exceptions but does not spell out a trade-secret carve-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: documented hazards — defective ignition switches, tainted drugs, unsafe machinery — often surface in lawsuits and then vanish behind sealed settlements, leaving future customers uninformed. The costs are real but modest: more judicial work before sealing, and less certainty for settling parties. The bill is narrowly drafted, applying only to cases where health or safety is at issue, with privacy and national security exceptions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 2014 on May 20, 2014, joined by original cosponsors including one Republican, Sen. Lindsey Graham.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that settle health and safety lawsuits kept the ability to hide evidence and settlement terms from the public and from regulators, since no new rules were ever enacted.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, drawing on his record as a consumer-protection litigator.

for.name: Sens. Lindsey Graham, Patrick Leahy, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship on the Senate Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 20, 2014 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed earlier versions of the Sunshine in Litigation Act, arguing it would undermine confidential settlements and trade-secret protection in litigation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan support from the start — one of its four cosponsors was a Republican — and died without any recorded vote, so no party split was ever measured on the floor.

industries.note: Litigation over drug and device safety often ends in settlements that keep adverse evidence sealed; the bill would let that evidence reach regulators and the public. Its interest in keeping settlements quiet runs against the public's interest in learning about hazards.
Defective-product cases are a main target of the bill; secrecy orders and gag settlements have historically concealed defects from future buyers. The bill would make those defects disclosable.

Lawyers for injured consumers could discuss the evidence and outcomes of health and safety cases without violating settlement terms, aiding future claims and public campaigns. Their interest runs alongside the public's.
